first_draft_paragraphs.text: FROM a darkness punctuated with throbbing stabs of fire, Tommy dragged his senses slowly back to life. When he at last opened his eyes, he was conscious of nothing but an excruciating pain through his temples. What the devil was the matter with his head?
“Damn!” said Tommy, and tried to sit up. He had remembered. He was in that sinister house in Soho. He uttered a groan and fell back. Through his almost-closed lids he reconnoitred carefully.

“He is coming to,” remarked a voice very near Tommy’s ear. He recognized it at once for that of the bearded and efficient German, and lay artistically inert. He felt that it would be a pity to come round too soon. Obviously somebody must have crept up behind him as he listened and struck him down with a blow on the head. They knew him now for a spy, and would in all probability give him short shrift. Nobody knew where he was, therefore he need expect no outside assistance, and must depend solely on his own wits.
“Well, here goes,” murmured Tommy to himself. “Damn!” he observed, and this time succeeded in sitting up.

In a minute the German stepped forward and placed a glass to his lips, with the brief command “Drink.” Tommy obeyed. The potency of the draught made him choke, but it cleared his brain in a marvellous manner.

He was lying on a couch in the room in which the meeting had been held. On one side of him was the German, on the other the villainous-faced doorkeeper who had let him in. The others were grouped together at a little distance away. But Tommy missed one face. The man known as Number One was no longer of the company.
“Feel better?” asked the German, as he removed the empty glass.
“Yes, thanks,” returned Tommy cheerfully.
“Ah, my young friend, it is lucky for you your skull is so thick. The good Conrad struck hard.” He indicated the evil-faced doorkeeper by a nod. The man grinned.
Tommy twisted his head round with an effort.
“Oh,” he said, “so you’re Conrad, are you? It strikes me the thickness of my skull was lucky for you too. When I look at you I feel it’s almost a pity I’ve enabled you to cheat the hangman.”

His manner was nonchalant to the last degree. Tommy Beresford was one of those young Englishmen not distinguished by any special intellectual ability, but who are emphatically at their best in what is known as a “tight place.” Their natural diffidence and caution fall from them like a glove. Tommy realized perfectly that in his own wits lay the only chance of escape, and behind his casual manner he was racking his brains furiously.
The cold accents of the German took up the conversation:
“Have you anything to say before you are put to death as a spy?”
“Simply lots of things,” replied Tommy with the same urbanity as before.
“How did you get in?” the German asked.
“Dear old Conrad here.” Tommy smiled deprecatingly at him. “I hesitate to suggest pensioning off a faithful servant, but you really ought to have a better watchdog.”
Conrad snarled impotently, and said sullenly, as the man with the beard swung round upon him:
“He gave the word. How was I to know?”
“Dead men tell no tales,” said the German evenly.
“Ah,” said Tommy, “but I’m not dead yet!”
Tommy’s heart beat faster, but his casual pleasantness did not waver.
“Can you give us any reason why we should not put you to death?” asked the German.
“Several,” replied Tommy. “Let me ask you one question for a change. Why didn’t you kill me off at once before I regained consciousness?”
The German hesitated, and Tommy seized his advantage.
“Because you didn’t know how much I knew--and where I obtained that knowledge. If you kill me now, you never will know.”
But here the emotions of Boris became too much for him. He stepped forward waving his arms.
“You hell-hound of a spy,” he screamed. “We will give you short shrift. Kill him! Kill him!”
There was a roar of applause.
“You hear?” said the German, his eyes on Tommy. “What have you to say to that?”

“Say?” Tommy shrugged his shoulders. “Pack of fools. Let them ask themselves a few questions. How did I get into this place? Remember what dear old Conrad said-- _with your own password_, wasn’t it? How did I get hold of that? You don’t suppose I came up those steps haphazard and said the first thing that came into my head?”
Tommy was pleased with the concluding words of this speech. His only regret was that Tuppence was not present to appreciate its full flavour.
“That is true,” said the working man suddenly. “Comrades, we have been betrayed!”
An ugly murmur arose.
“You will tell us who has betrayed us,” said the German. “But that shall not save you--oh, no! You shall tell us all that you know. Boris, here, knows pretty ways of making people speak!”
“Bah!” said Tommy scornfully, fighting down a singularly unpleasant feeling in the pit of his stomach. “You will neither torture me nor kill me.”
“And why not?” asked Boris.
“Because you’d kill the goose that lays the golden eggs,” replied Tommy quietly.
There was a momentary pause. They were no longer completely sure of themselves. The man in the shabby clothes stared at Tommy searchingly.
“He’s bluffing you, Boris,” he said quietly.
Tommy hated him. Had the man seen through him?
Suddenly Boris stepped forward, and shook his fist in Tommy’s face.
“Speak, you swine of an Englishman--speak!”
“Don’t get so excited, my good fellow,” said Tommy calmly. “Do I look as though I thought there were the least chance of your killing me?”
He looked confidently round, and was glad they could not hear the persistent beating of his heart which gave the lie to his words.
“No,” admitted Boris at last sullenly, “you do not.”
“Thank God, he’s not a mind reader,” thought Tommy. Aloud he pursued his advantage:
“And why am I so confident? Because I know something that puts me in a position to propose a bargain.”
“A bargain?” The bearded man took him up sharply.
“Yes--a bargain. My life and liberty against----” He paused.
“Against what?”
The group pressed forward. You could have heard a pin drop.
Slowly Tommy spoke.
“The papers that Danvers brought over from America in the _Lusitania_.”
The effect of his words was electrical. Every one was on his feet. The German leaned over Tommy, his face purple with excitement.
“_Himmel!_ You have got them, then?”
With magnificent calm Tommy shook his head.
“You know where they are?” persisted the German.
Again Tommy shook his head. “Not in the least.”
“Then--then----” angry and baffled, the words failed him.
“I don’t know where the papers are--but I believe that I can find them. I have a theory----” Tommy went on.
“Pah!”
Tommy raised his hand, and silenced the clamours of disgust.
“I call it a theory--but I’m pretty sure of my facts--facts that are known to no one but myself. If I can produce the papers--you give me my life and liberty in exchange. Is it a bargain?”
“And if we refuse?” said the German quietly.
Tommy lay back on the couch.
“The 29th,” he said thoughtfully, “is less than a fortnight ahead----”
For a moment the German hesitated. Then he made a sign to Conrad.
“Take him into the other room.”

For five minutes, Tommy sat on the bed in the dingy room next door. His heart was beating violently. He had risked all on this throw. How would they decide? And all the while he talked flippantly to Conrad, enraging the cross-grained doorkeeper to the point of homicidal mania.
At last the German called imperiously to Conrad to return.
“Let’s hope the judge hasn’t put his black cap on,” remarked Tommy frivolously. “That’s right, Conrad, march me in. The prisoner is at the bar, gentlemen.”
The German was seated once more behind the table.
“We accept,” he said harshly, “on terms. The papers must be delivered to us before you go free.”
“Idiot!” said Tommy amiably. “How do you think I can look for them if you keep me tied by the leg here?”

“We prefer,” said the German coldly, “that you should remain here. One of our number will carry out your instructions minutely. If the operations are complicated, he will return to you with a report and you can instruct him further.”
“You’re tying my hands,” complained Tommy. “It’s a very delicate affair, and the other fellow will muff it up as likely as not.”
The German rapped the table.
“Those are our terms. Otherwise, death!”
Tommy leaned back wearily.
“I like your style. Curt, but attractive. So be it, then. But one thing is essential, I must see the girl.”
“What girl?”
“Jane Finn, of course.”
The other looked at him curiously for some minutes, then he said slowly, and as though choosing his words with care:
“Do you not know that she can tell you nothing?”
Tommy’s heart beat a little faster. Would he succeed in coming face to face with the girl he was seeking?
“I shall not ask her to tell me anything,” he said quietly. “Not in so many words, that is.”
“Then why see her?”
Tommy paused.
“To watch her face when I ask her one question,” he replied at last.
Again there was a look in the German’s eyes that Tommy did not quite understand.
“She will not be able to answer your question.”
“That does not matter. I shall have seen her face when I ask it.”

“And you think that will tell you anything?” He gave a short disagreeable laugh. More than ever, Tommy felt that there was a factor somewhere that he did not understand. “I wonder whether, after all, you know as much as we think?” the German said softly.
Tommy felt his ascendancy less sure. His hold had slipped a little. What had he said wrong? He spoke out on the impulse of the moment.

“There may be things that you know which I do not. But equally I’ve got something up my sleeve that _you_ don’t know about. Danvers was a damned clever fellow----” He broke off as if he had said too much.
But the German’s face had lightened a little.
“Danvers,” he murmured. “I see----” He waved to Conrad. “Take him away. Upstairs--you know.”
“Wait a minute,” said Tommy. “What about the girl?”
“We will see about it. Only one person can decide that.”
“Who?” asked Tommy. But he knew the answer.
“Mr. Brown----”
“Shall I see him?”
“Perhaps.”
“Come,” said Conrad harshly.
On the floor above Conrad opened a door and Tommy passed into a small room. Conrad lit a hissing gas burner and went out. Tommy heard the sound of the key being turned in the lock.

There was something peculiarly airless about the atmosphere. Then he realized that there was no window. The walls were filthily dirty. Four pictures hung crookedly on the wall representing scenes from Faust. Marguerite with her box of jewels, the church scene, Siebel and his flowers, and Faust and Mephistopheles. The latter brought Tommy’s mind back to Mr. Brown again. In this sealed and closed chamber he felt cut off from the world, and the sinister power of the arch-criminal seemed more real. Shout as he would, no one could ever hear him. The place was a living tomb....
With an effort Tommy pulled himself together. He sank on to the bed. His head ached badly; also, he was hungry.
“Anyway,” said Tommy, trying to cheer himself, “I shall see the chief--the mysterious Mr. Brown and with a bit of luck in bluffing I shall see the mysterious Jane Finn also. After that----”
After that Tommy was forced to admit the prospect looked dreary.

FROM a darkness punctuated with throbbing stabs of fire, Tommy dragged
his senses slowly back to life. When he at last opened his eyes, he was
conscious of nothing but an excruciating pain through his temples. He
was vaguely aware of unfamiliar surroundings. Where was he? What had
happened? He blinked feebly. This was not his bedroom at the _Ritz_. And
what the devil was the matter with his head?

“Damn!” said Tommy, and tried to sit up. He had remembered. He was in
that sinister house in Soho. He uttered a groan and fell back. Through
his almost-closed lids he reconnoitred carefully.

“He is coming to,” remarked a voice very near Tommy’s ear. He recognized
it at once for that of the bearded and efficient German, and lay
artistically inert. He felt that it would be a pity to come round too
soon; and until the pain in his head became a little less acute, he felt
quite incapable of collecting his wits. Painfully he tried to puzzle out
what had happened. Obviously somebody must have crept up behind him as
he listened and struck him down with a blow on the head. They knew
him now for a spy, and would in all probability give him short shrift.
Undoubtedly he was in a tight place. Nobody knew where he was, therefore
he need expect no outside assistance, and must depend solely on his own
wits.

“Well, here goes,” murmured Tommy to himself, and repeated his former
remark.

“Damn!” he observed, and this time succeeded in sitting up.

In a minute the German stepped forward and placed a glass to his lips,
with the brief command “Drink.” Tommy obeyed. The potency of the draught
made him choke, but it cleared his brain in a marvellous manner.

He was lying on a couch in the room in which the meeting had been held.
On one side of him was the German, on the other the villainous-faced
doorkeeper who had let him in. The others were grouped together at a
little distance away. But Tommy missed one face. The man known as Number
One was no longer of the company.

“Feel better?” asked the German, as he removed the empty glass.

“Yes, thanks,” returned Tommy cheerfully.

“Ah, my young friend, it is lucky for you your skull is so thick. The
good Conrad struck hard.” He indicated the evil-faced doorkeeper by a
nod. The man grinned.

Tommy twisted his head round with an effort.

“Oh,” he said, “so you’re Conrad, are you? It strikes me the thickness
of my skull was lucky for you too. When I look at you I feel it’s almost
a pity I’ve enabled you to cheat the hangman.”

The man snarled, and the bearded man said quietly:

“He would have run no risk of that.”

“Just as you like,” replied Tommy. “I know it’s the fashion to run down
the police. I rather believe in them myself.”

His manner was nonchalant to the last degree. Tommy Beresford was one

The cold accents of the German took up the conversation:

“Simply lots of things,” replied Tommy with the same urbanity as before.

“Do you deny that you were listening at that door?”

“I do not. I must really apologize--but your conversation was so
interesting that it overcame my scruples.”

“How did you get in?”

“Dear old Conrad here.” Tommy smiled deprecatingly at him. “I hesitate
to suggest pensioning off a faithful servant, but you really ought to
have a better watchdog.”

Conrad snarled impotently, and said sullenly, as the man with the beard
swung round upon him:

“He gave the word. How was I to know?”

“Yes,” Tommy chimed in. “How was he to know? Don’t blame the poor
fellow. His hasty action has given me the pleasure of seeing you all
face to face.”

He fancied that his words caused some discomposure among the group, but
the watchful German stilled it with a wave of his hand.

“Dead men tell no tales,” he said evenly.

“Ah,” said Tommy, “but I’m not dead yet!”

“You soon will be, my young friend,” said the German.

An assenting murmur came from the others.

Tommy’s heart beat faster, but his casual pleasantness did not waver.

“I think not,” he said firmly. “I should have a great objection to
dying.”

He had got them puzzled, he saw that by the look on his captor’s face.

“Can you give us any reason why we should not put you to death?” asked

“Several,” replied Tommy. “Look here, you’ve been asking me a lot of

The German hesitated, and Tommy seized his advantage.

“You hell-hound of a spy,” he screamed. “We will give you short shrift.
Kill him! Kill him!”

“You hear?” said the German, his eyes on Tommy. “What have you to say to

“That is true,” said the working man suddenly. “Comrades, we have been

An ugly murmur arose. Tommy smiled at them encouragingly.

“Yes--a bargain. My life and liberty against----” He paused.

“Against what?”

The group pressed forward. You could have heard a pin drop.

Slowly Tommy spoke.

“The papers that Danvers brought over from America in the _Lusitania_.”

The effect of his words was electrical. Every one was on his feet.
The German waved them back. He leaned over Tommy, his face purple with

With magnificent calm Tommy shook his head.

“You know where they are?” persisted the German.

Again Tommy shook his head. “Not in the least.”

“Then--then----” angry and baffled, the words failed him.

Tommy looked round. He saw anger and bewilderment on every face, but his
calm assurance had done its work--no one doubted but that something lay
behind his words.

“I don’t know where the papers are--but I believe that I can find them.
I have a theory----”

“Pah!”

Tommy raised his hand, and silenced the clamours of disgust.

“I call it a theory--but I’m pretty sure of my facts--facts that are
known to no one but myself. In any case what do you lose? If I can

bargain?”

“And if we refuse?” said the German quietly.

Tommy lay back on the couch.

“The 29th,” he said thoughtfully, “is less than a fortnight ahead----”

For a moment the German hesitated. Then he made a sign to Conrad.

“Take him into the other room.”

For five minutes, Tommy sat on the bed in the dingy room next door. His

they decide? And all the while that this agonized questioning went on
within him, he talked flippantly to Conrad, enraging the cross-grained

At last the door opened, and the German called imperiously to Conrad to

“Let’s hope the judge hasn’t put his black cap on,” remarked Tommy
frivolously. “That’s right, Conrad, march me in. The prisoner is at the
bar, gentlemen.”

The German was seated once more behind the table. He motioned to Tommy

“We accept,” he said harshly, “on terms. The papers must be delivered to
us before you go free.”

“Idiot!” said Tommy amiably. “How do you think I can look for them if
you keep me tied by the leg here?”

“What do you expect, then?”

“I must have liberty to go about the business in my own way.”

The German laughed.

“Do you think we are little children to let you walk out of here leaving
us a pretty story full of promises?”

“No,” said Tommy thoughtfully. “Though infinitely simpler for me, I
did not really think you would agree to that plan. Very well, we must
arrange a compromise. How would it be if you attached little Conrad here
to my person. He’s a faithful fellow, and very ready with the fist.”

“We prefer,” said the German coldly, “that you should remain here.
One of our number will carry out your instructions minutely. If the

“You’re tying my hands,” complained Tommy. “It’s a very delicate affair,

The German rapped the table.

Tommy leaned back wearily.

“She will not be able to answer your question.”

“That does not matter. I shall have seen her face when I ask it.”

“There may be things that you know which I do not. I have not pretended

atmosphere of it. Then he realized that there was no window. He walked
round it. The walls were filthily dirty, as everywhere else. Four
pictures hung crookedly on the wall representing scenes from Faust.
Marguerite with her box of jewels, the church scene, Siebel and his

preservation_plan.book_context: A 1919-era thriller structured as alternating threads: Tommy's captivity, Tuppence's investigations, and Julius's hustle. Every chapter plants clues that pay off in the final unmasking. Recurring mechanisms include bluffing with ignorance, telegrams and notes as decoys, concealment between allies ('Never tell all you know'), and the Mr. Brown motif of an ordinary, unseen chief. Chapters XVI–XIX carry the plot from Tommy's bluff in the Soho house, through his escape with the help of 'Annette', to the bogus telegram that lures Tuppence away and Sir James's 'discovery' of Jane Finn in Manchester. These chapters seed several later reveals: the Faust picture as hiding place, the Marguerite cry, Annette as the real Jane, Charing Cross versus the altered telegram, the 'Twopence' signature test, the Sunday timing of Tommy's exposure, the staged Manchester girl, and Sir James as Mr. Brown. The abridgment must keep these clues present but unexplained in the chapters where they first appear.
continuity_checks: Conrad is named here for the first time as the man who struck Tommy and who let him in.
Number One (Kramenin, unnamed until the next chapter) must be absent. Do not name him.
Tommy has no papers and no location for them, only a claimed 'theory'.
Neither Tommy nor the narrator explains that Jane has lost her memory.
Boris is present and identified by name.

dependencies.instruction: Name all four Faust pictures, especially Marguerite with her jewels, as neutral room description. Give no hint that anything is hidden behind them.
dependencies.local_evidence: Marguerite with her box of jewels
dependencies.other_evidence: Very gently, I unhooked one of the pictures from its nail--Marguerite with her casket of jewels.

dependencies.instruction: Keep the German's curious look and Tommy's sense of 'a factor somewhere that he did not understand'. Do not explain the loss of memory from Tommy's point of view.
dependencies.local_evidence: “Do you not know that she can tell you nothing?”
dependencies.other_evidence: By Jove, that explains why they looked at me so queerly when I spoke of questioning her.

dependencies.instruction: Keep the date as Tommy's lever, drawn from what he overheard at the meeting.
dependencies.local_evidence: “The 29th,” he said thoughtfully, “is less than a fortnight ahead----”

essential: Tommy wakes in pain in the Soho house and recognises the German's voice. He feigns unconsciousness briefly, then is revived with a drink.
Establish who is present: the German, Conrad named as the doorkeeper who struck him, Boris, and the others. Number One is absent.
Tommy's nonchalant banter with Conrad and the German (the thick skull, the faithful watchdog) masks frantic calculation. Keep both layers: outward flippancy and inner fear.
Keep the logical chain of the bluff: they did not kill him at once because they do not know what he knows or where he learned it.
Boris screams 'Kill him!'. Tommy counters with the password point, which prompts the working man's 'Comrades, we have been betrayed!'.
The German threatens Boris's 'pretty ways'. The shabby clerk-like man says 'He's bluffing you, Boris', and Tommy fears he has been seen through.

Tommy states the bargain: his life and liberty against the Danvers papers. He has neither the papers nor their location, only a 'theory'. He adds the pressure of 'The 29th' being less than a fortnight away.
Keep the deliberation interval: Tommy waits in the next room, flippant with Conrad, while his heart beats violently. Keep the black-cap joke.
State the terms: Tommy stays prisoner and a gang member carries out his instructions. Tommy grumbles but accepts.
Tommy demands to see Jane Finn. The German's puzzling replies make Tommy feel his hold slipping. He recovers with 'Danvers was a damned clever fellow----', which reassures the German.
Only Mr. Brown can decide about the girl. 'Shall I see him?' 'Perhaps.'
Tommy is locked in a windowless upstairs room with the four Faust pictures. Mephistopheles suggests Mr. Brown, the room is a living tomb, and the chapter ends on Tommy's dreary hopes.
optional: Shorten the opening sensory paragraph (para 1) to a sentence or two.
Compress the 'cheat the hangman' and 'I rather believe in [the police]' exchange (paras 12–15) into one retort.
Shorten the 'Dead men tell no tales' / 'not dead yet' / 'great objection to dying' run (paras 28–33), keeping one or two lines.
The 'Don't get so excited... you foreigners' speech and Boris's 'No... you do not' (paras 58–63) may be condensed. Keep the 'Thank God, he's not a mind reader' inner aside if space allows.
The compromise offer of attaching Conrad to him (para 97) and the 'ounce of tact' complaint (para 99) can be cut together.
Paragraph 132 (headache, hunger) can be cut, but hunger must be mentioned somewhere because the next chapter opens on it.
risks: Including the deliberation interval may push the bargain sections over budget. Trim the banter before cutting logical steps.

preservation_plan.title: FURTHER ADVENTURES OF TOMMY

verbatim.purpose: Signature narratorial generalisation defining Tommy's character, echoed in Carter's later assessment.
verbatim.text: Tommy Beresford was one of those young Englishmen not distinguished by any special intellectual ability, but who are emphatically at their best in what is known as a “tight place.”

verbatim.purpose: Hinge of the bluff: turns his chance entry into a suggestion of betrayal.
verbatim.text: Remember what dear old Conrad said-- _with your own password_, wasn’t it? How did I get hold of that?

verbatim.purpose: Comic self-awareness, and the partnership kept alive while the two are apart.
verbatim.text: His only regret was that Tuppence was not present to appreciate its full flavour.

verbatim.purpose: Core of the leverage argument, in Tommy's understated idiom.
verbatim.text: “Because you’d kill the goose that lays the golden eggs,” replied Tommy quietly.

verbatim.purpose: The climactic bargaining chip; its effect is 'electrical'.
verbatim.text: “The papers that Danvers brought over from America in the _Lusitania_.”

verbatim.purpose: Ambiguous hint, unexplained to Tommy, that later reveals his slip about Jane's memory.
verbatim.text: “Do you not know that she can tell you nothing?”

verbatim.purpose: Tommy's improvised reason for seeing Jane; it exposes the gap in his knowledge.
verbatim.text: “To watch her face when I ask her one question,” he replied at last.

verbatim.purpose: Plants the hiding place of the treaty and the source of the 'Marguerite' clue.
verbatim.text: Four pictures hung crookedly on the wall representing scenes from Faust. Marguerite with her box of jewels, the church scene, Siebel and his flowers, and Faust and Mephistopheles.

preservation_plan.voice_profile: Brisk, ironic third-person narration that stays close to Tommy, and later to Tommy and Julius, in the 'Young Adventurers' manner. The comedy comes from undercutting: Tommy's flippant, schoolboy bravado ('old bean', mock-heroic asides, 'Retire, varlet') is set against honest admissions of fear ('glad they could not hear the persistent beating of his heart'). Narrative generalisation about types ('one of those young Englishmen...') and cinema or dime-novel self-consciousness recur. Dialogue does most of the work. National idiom marks each speaker: Julius's Americanisms ('Put me wise', 'Sure thing', 'gets my goat'), the German's clipped menace, Conrad's and Number 14's cockney, Annette's broken English and French. Sir James speaks in dry, evasive legal phrasing ('Coincidences are curious things'). Chapters end on hooks: a reversal, a telegram, a twist. Double-hyphen dashes, '----' for broken-off speech and underscore emphasis are characteristic and must be retained.
